what: Hafnia owns and operates one of the world’s largest fleets of product tankers, ships that carry refined fuels such as diesel, petrol, jet fuel and naphtha, along with some chemicals and vegetable oils. It also runs pools that manage ships for other owners.
customers: Oil majors, refiners and commodity traders who charter ships to move refined products between refineries and markets.
money: Charter income from its own and pooled ships, mostly at spot rates that change week to week.
Fees for managing other owners’ ships in its pools, and bunker procurement.
moat: Size. Running about 200 ships in pools gives Hafnia better utilisation, more cargo options and lower costs per ship than small owners, but no pricing power: the freight rate is set by the market for everyone.
risks: Rates are cyclical and can fall fast. Net income fell from $774M in 2024 to $340M in 2025 when rates eased.
New ships ordered in recent years will add to supply.
Much of the strength in product tanker rates comes from trade disruption: sanctions on Russian fuel and longer routes around the Red Sea. If those ease, routes shorten and rates fall.
Only two analysts cover the stock, so there is little independent research.
opportunities: At about six times trailing earnings and a 12.6% dividend yield, the price assumes a sharp downturn.
Trailing net income of $738M is back near 2024’s level, so rates have recovered from the 2025 dip.
Debt of $974M against $3.1B of equity is modest for a shipowner.
Hafnia pays out a large share of its profit, so shareholders see the cycle in cash.
watch: Product tanker spot rates, and whether new ship deliveries start to outpace demand.
view: Hafnia is a pure bet on the price of shipping refined fuel, and it returns most of what it earns, so the dividend is the investment. At six times trailing earnings and a double-digit yield, the market is not paying for the current profit; it is assuming that profit halves, as it did in 2025, when net income fell from $774 million to $340 million.

That assumption is not unreasonable. Today’s rates are propped up by politics as much as by demand: Russian product exports go the long way round, and Red Sea diversions add weeks to voyages. Every one of those disruptions has an end date nobody can predict. On the other side, the fleet is old, scrapping is overdue and refineries keep closing in Europe and opening in the Middle East and Asia, which lengthens the average voyage for years.

The one thing this turns on is the rate cycle, and nobody forecasts that well, including me. What makes Hafnia reasonable rather than reckless is the balance sheet: under a billion of debt against $3 billion of equity means a bad year cuts the dividend, not the company. I would size it as a cyclical income position, expect the payout to swing, and not mistake a six-times P/E for a bargain.
bull: Disruptions and an ageing fleet keep rates high, and Hafnia keeps paying a double-digit yield.
bear: Trade routes normalise, new ships arrive and earnings and the dividend halve again.
